title: Who ran it, who built it and who said no
lede: Titles are as given in the filings and the press at the time. Later careers are left out where we have no source.

people.name: William M. “Trip” Hawkins III
people.text: An early Apple employee who founded Electronic Arts in 1982 and gave up its chairmanship in 1994 to run 3DO. He had put $15M of his own money in by late 1994, owned about 38% of the shares in 2002, lent the company money in its last months and bought two lots at its auction.[^7][^10][^16][^22][^23]
people.later: Described in 2014 as the founder of Electronic Arts and Digital Chocolate, when he became an adviser to the mobile company Skillz.[^38]

people.name: Hugh Martin
people.text: Chief operating officer from January 1993. He took full operating control in the September 1996 reorganization, when Hawkins moved to a creative role.[^2][^25]

people.name: Dave Needle and RJ Mical
people.text: Named in 3DO’s filings as parties, with NTG Engineering, to the 1993 agreements under which 3DO acquired NTG for $21.4M in stock and cash.[^1]

people.name: Bob Faber
people.role: Senior vice president, sales and marketing, 1993
people.text: Said he “sighed with relief” when Nintendo and Silicon Graphics announced their console partnership in August 1993, because it showed they were starting from scratch.[^20]

people.name: John Adams
people.text: His plan to leave was announced with the June 2000 profit warning.[^27]

people.name: Vinod Khosla
people.text: The venture capitalist told the Times in 1994, after the developer surcharge: “Trip doesn’t appreciate the finer nuances of social relationships.”[^23]

people.name: Yoichi Morishita
people.text: Announced in July 1997 that Matsushita had stopped developing the M2 console it had paid 3DO $100M to license.[^1][^26]
